When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

segment:
Her heart stuttered. She knew that face. Hadn’t seen it in years but recognized it like a brother.
For a while they looked at each other; the longer she stood there, the surer she was that he didn’t recognize her. But he had to know that she knew him; it showed, somewhere on her face. She kept staring.
“You’re early.” His voice, low and faintly amused: familiar. She swallowed.
She looked away, realizing suddenly that he was watching her mouth. “Yeah.” The breath came easy now.
He smiled but still didn’t get up.
“How’s it going?”
“Good.”
They stood in silence for another minute or two. Mara’s back was starting to ache. It didn’t help that she was wearing a pack, too.
Finally she asked, “Do we all just sit around and wait? Is that the procedure? Or do we eat?”
He nodded slightly but stayed still, evidently not ready to answer.
A few moments later someone else entered the room—a man in his fifties, carrying a small black notebook. When Mara turned away from the couch she was startled to see him there, watching her. But she wasn’t surprised; she knew who he was.
He gave them both a tight smile, waved, and went around the table to his chair. Then he took off his glasses and opened his book.

segment:
A man, it turned out. Maybe twenty-four or twenty-five? In the same gray cotton T-shirt as the welcome pack that she’d carried in her backpack to the gate, with blue-green eyes and a faint smile that seemed to mean nothing at all. She watched his gaze fall past her head to the entryway, then back.
“Welcome, Mara.”
His voice was low and musical. “Hi.” She tried to steady her breathing, to not look so stiffly out of place. She dropped her pack by the door, then took a slow step inside, hands hanging loose and empty.
“I’m glad you came,” he continued, as though the first words hadn’t been enough.
She waited for him to continue, to introduce himself or say something more; she wanted to know who he was and what he did here. But when he didn’t, she cleared her throat and ventured, “Who are you?”
A faint smile quirked his lips. “That’s not a name,” he said softly.
“What’s yours, then?”
He laughed a little, shaking his head. “Mine?” he asked quietly. “Oh, I guess it depends on what you’d like me to be called.”

segment:
“They tell me to expect you around this time, so I’ve come to say hello.”
“Good evening,” Mara returned. Her voice sounded much louder than he would need.
His right arm lifted; the hand spread, palm up. “Adrian said I was your type.”
“So it seems.”
He grinned, leaning forward with hands flat on the table, elbows apart, and the bare legs uncrossing at a deliberate pace. “You’re much prettier than I thought.”
“So am I,” she said; her voice had the edge of a laugh, but the statement was true. She crossed the room toward him, aware of the body moving in response.
When she reached the table she saw his eyes take her in, her hair and dress and earrings and the bare feet, one after the other without any hint of disapproval. His face was a study of admiration; it made her uneasy, but not uneasy enough to stop walking.
“Do you want me to sit?” he asked. “I’d rather stand.”
“Fine with me,” he said. She sat on the arm of his chair and watched as he leaned forward again and studied her bare legs.
She put down her cup. “Do you always do this, Jonah?”
He was frowning slightly, but he didn’t stop watching her. “You know I like to. Why are you asking now?”
“Because I’ve had enough.” She reached out to touch his hand and he flinched.
“Are you all right?” she asked.
“Fine, I said. Just surprised is all.” He made a sound somewhere between a sigh and a chuckle. “Well, don’t worry about it.”

segment:
“I was expecting someone else,” Mara said, still holding her ground, “someone more like a teacher.”
“A teacher of what?” the blond man asked.
“Of reading faces or something like that. She’s called Livia Sloane.”
“Yes.”
“I don’t think you are Livia.”
He smiled at her, slightly, like a cat with an open box. She had seen that expression in online videos.
She had studied dozens of those videos over the last week. None of them had actually prepared her for this.
“Well,” she said, “I’m glad that it’s not her. I don’t know about you, but if I’m going to be stuck in here all night, I’d rather look at you.”
The blond man let the smile play a little longer, then glanced away.
“I’m glad that I’m not the object of your attention.”
She realized suddenly how she was standing there in the doorway, so unselfconsciously watchful; how she had been watching him all along with this cold, frank stare, as though he were a display animal in a zoo or a criminal on the witness stand.
He was probably used to being stared at that way; it came with the territory. She felt a sudden tenderness and anger toward him for this, an urge to do something kind for him, and also an urge to hurt him.

segment:
He didn’t sit up or stand up, and his dark eyes said nothing of whether he intended to.
She saw her reflection in the black windows. The shadows were deep, but she saw her pale blue blouse with the loose bow at the neck, her dark cropped hair, her bare arms, and her dark trousers. She felt her breath again.
“No, you’re not,” he said, after a long while.
She blinked at him. “Excuse me?”
“You’re not Adrian.”
That seemed like an accurate enough assessment of reality, though she’d expected more of a greeting. “No, I’m Mara. Nice to meet you.” She offered her hand. He didn’t take it, or move an inch, just kept looking at her as if she were some strange species, and she didn’t retract hers right away. She felt like an idiot. She turned to face the door and realized there was an open door at the other end of the common room too. He might be waiting for Adrian to come in through the other one.
She cleared her throat and said, “Sorry, I thought this was where we were meant to be.”
“I didn’t say you weren’t. I said you were not Adrian. So it looks like we’re both waiting.”

NEW MOVEMENT

Dramatic design for the next prose movement
Continue from the present welcome without replaying Mara's arrival. The unnamed blond man is Jonah; Mara may learn his name through the exchange. Render one first dyadic contact through concrete dialogue, posture, and an imperfect inference. The exchange changes what Mara attends to without resolving whom she can trust. Adrian remains elsewhere and is neither seen nor mentioned.
